# True or false: Security

Vulnerabilities, secrets, dependencies, zero trust and the quantum timeline. Separate the controls that work from the ones that only feel safe.

11 statements (Foundation 3, Standard 7, Assured 1). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area security`.

### 1. A vulnerability with a medium CVSS score can be more urgent than one scored 9.8.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Severity scores say how bad a vulnerability could be, not whether anyone is exploiting it. A medium-scored flaw listed in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on an internet-facing system beats an unexploited 9.8 on an internal one. Combine the severity score with EPSS (the estimated chance of exploitation), KEV and exposure, and fix KEV entries on internet-facing systems within 72 hours.

Read more: [playbook/security/vulnerability-management.md](../../playbook/security/vulnerability-management.md)

</details>

### 2. If a secret is committed to git, removing it with a force-push makes it safe again.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A pushed secret lives on in every clone, fork and cache, so assume someone has copied it. Revoke and rotate the secret first. Then clean the history if you want to.

Read more: [playbook/security/secrets.md](../../playbook/security/secrets.md)

</details>

### 3. Security keys and passkeys resist phishing in a way that SMS codes do not.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** An attacker can phish an SMS code through a fake login page or intercept it, while a security key or passkey is bound to the real site. The playbook requires phishing-resistant MFA for anything that touches production. Make admin rights temporary as well.

Read more: [playbook/security/access-control.md](../../playbook/security/access-control.md)

</details>

### 4. An organisation can achieve zero trust by buying a zero trust product.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Zero trust is a set of changes across five pillars in the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model: identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, and data. A product can help with one pillar. Start with identity and MFA, and show progress per pillar every quarter.

Read more: [playbook/security/zero-trust.md](../../playbook/security/zero-trust.md)

</details>

### 5. Internal APIs do not need authentication because they sit behind the firewall.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** On a flat internal network, one phished laptop or compromised server can reach everything. Give each workload its own identity and authorise every call. NIST SP 800-207 grants no implicit trust based on network location.

Read more: [playbook/security/zero-trust.md](../../playbook/security/zero-trust.md)

</details>

### 6. There is no need to start post-quantum work until a large quantum computer exists.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Attackers can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it later, so long-lived secrets are already exposed. NIST plans to deprecate RSA and elliptic-curve algorithms after 2030 and disallow them after 2035. Past cryptographic migrations took 10 to 20 years, so start with an inventory now.

Read more: [playbook/security/post-quantum-readiness.md](../../playbook/security/post-quantum-readiness.md)

</details>

### 7. AES-256 does not need to be replaced to stay safe against quantum computers.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** NIST believes approved symmetric algorithms with at least 128 bits of classical security meet its lowest post-quantum security category. The urgent risk is public-key cryptography such as RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange. Spend the effort on key exchange and signatures, starting with hybrid key exchange that includes the new NIST standard ML-KEM.

Read more: [playbook/security/post-quantum-readiness.md](../../playbook/security/post-quantum-readiness.md)

</details>

### 8. Applications should commit their dependency lockfile and install from it in CI.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Version ranges without a lockfile mean two builds of the same commit can pull different code. The lockfile pins exactly what was tested. An update bot then proposes changes in small, reviewable steps.

Read more: [playbook/security/dependencies.md](../../playbook/security/dependencies.md)

</details>

### 9. Signing build artifacts protects you even if nothing checks the signatures at deployment.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A signature nobody verifies stops nothing. Check signatures at admission, so unverified artifacts do not run. Keep the signing key out of reach of ordinary CI jobs, or use keyless signing.

Read more: [playbook/security/supply-chain.md](../../playbook/security/supply-chain.md)

</details>

### 10. A yearly penetration test cannot replace security checks that run on every change.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A pen test finds what the pipeline missed; it does not replace the pipeline. Model threats at design time and run security checks on every pull request. Those checks cost minutes, while issues found by attackers cost weeks.

Read more: [playbook/security/secure-development.md](../../playbook/security/secure-development.md)

</details>

### 11. CI actions should be pinned to a full commit hash (SHA) rather than a tag such as @v4.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A tag can be moved to point at different code, including malicious code, without any change in your repository. A full commit hash cannot. Keep the version in a comment and let an update bot bump the hash.

Read more: [playbook/security/supply-chain.md](../../playbook/security/supply-chain.md)

</details>
